docs.title: bteng-nav2
docs.text:
bteng-nav2 is a Python library of Nav2 behavior tree nodes built on top of bteng and bteng-ros2 — and a command that runs trees, so a project can need no application Python at all.

It provides ready-made action, service, condition, and publisher nodes that wrap the standard Nav2 ROS 2 interfaces. Drop them into any bteng tree alongside your own custom nodes to build navigation behaviors — patrol routes, recovery sequences, docking procedures — without writing boilerplate action client or service client code.

docs.title: Run a tree with one command
docs.text:
A params file, a tree, and bteng-nav2 run. No Python, no colcon, no workspace:

bteng-nav2 run trees/ -p params.yaml              # every tree in the directory
bteng-nav2 run trees/ -p params.yaml --dry-run    # parse + build only: a CI gate, no robot
bteng-nav2 run trees/ -p params.yaml --namespace /robot1
bteng-nav2 nodes                                  # every XML tag this package registers

--dry-run builds every tree, types every seeded value and needs no ROS installation at all, which makes it usable as a pull-request check. Full reference: Running from the CLI.

docs.title: Key features
docs.text:
• One command — bteng-nav2 run trees/ -p params.yaml; a consuming project ships params and XML only
  • 13 action nodes — NavigateToPose, NavigateThroughPoses, ComputePathToPose, ComputePathThroughPoses, FollowPath, SmoothPath, Spin, BackUp, DriveOnHeading, Wait, AssistedTeleop, DockRobot, UndockRobot
  • 8 service nodes — ClearGlobalCostmap, ClearLocalCostmap, ClearGlobalCostmapAroundRobot, ClearLocalCostmapAroundRobot, GetGlobalCostmap, GetLocalCostmap, IsPathValid, LoadMap
  • 6 condition nodes — IsRobotNearGoal, IsLocalizationActive, IsObstacleNear, IsStuck, IsGoalUpdated, IsNavigationActive
  • 2 publisher nodes — PublishGoalPose, SetInitialPose
  • Retargetable endpoints — every action, service and condition node takes its server or topic as a port, so a second planner or a per-robot namespace is a tree change, not a subclass (Retargeting endpoints)
  • Blackboard-based port wiring — all inputs and outputs flow through the bteng blackboard
  • Offline-testable — the test suite runs without a ROS 2 installation using the bundled stub layer

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install bteng-nav2

With ROS 2 sourced in your environment:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
pip install bteng-nav2

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• bteng>=0.3.2, bteng-ros2>=0.3.0, raised from 0.3.1 / 0.2.3. Nothing here needs the newer code — all 481 tests and all five example trees pass unchanged on either — but 0.3.2 and 0.3.0 are the first releases of each requiring Python 3.12, and the old floors let pip install bteng-ros2 resolve to 0.2.4 + bteng 0.3.1 on a 3.10/3.11 interpreter. CI was doing exactly that: its 3.10 and 3.11 legs tested a different engine than its 3.12 leg. The behaviour floors are still 0.3.1 and 0.2.3, and the docs now say so.
  • requires-python = ">=3.12", and the CI matrix drops to ["3.12"] from ["3.10", "3.11", "3.12"].

[!WARNING] This drops ROS 2 Humble and Iron, which ship Python 3.10. Jazzy onward only. It is a deliberate trade — consistency with the engine over LTS reach. Humble users pin bteng-nav2==0.2.4, which runs on bteng 0.3.1.

  • ruff target-version follows to py312.

docs.title: Removed
docs.text: • bteng_nav2/py.typed. The marker promised verified annotations that nothing verifies: CI runs ruff and pytest with no type checker, and neither bteng nor bteng-ros2 ships a marker, so every imported symbol resolved to Any regardless. The annotations are untouched — only the marker and its package-data entry are gone.

docs.title: Verified
docs.text: Against bteng 0.3.2: 481 passed, 14 skipped (the same 14 as on 0.3.1 — costmap and map service nodes needing typed messages). --dry-run builds and Tree.validate()s all five example trees with output identical to 0.3.1. The two control-node attributes in those trees, <Retry num_attempts="2"> and <Timeout msec="120000">, are literals, so 0.3.2's change to bind {key} references on control and decorator attributes does not reach them.

docs.title: Fixed: seven defects the first runs against a real ROS graph produced
docs.text:
Everything in this package had only ever run against stubs. Run against ROS 2 Jazzy with real rclpy and real DDS -- stub servers on the Nav2 endpoints, no simulator, since what was missing was a wire -- three defects appeared immediately, a fourth once the stub grew the endpoints the last two trees needed, and three more once every one of the 38 node types was exercised. All seven passed the full offline suite and --dry-run first.

start was required, though everything documents it as optional. InputPort("start", default=None) declares a required port: BTEng reads a None default as "this port has no default". So every tree that planned from the robot's current pose -- the documented behaviour, and what make_goal() implements -- was rejected at executor construction. 02_compute_and_follow.xml, shipped in this repo, was one of them. Optional ports now default to "". goal_pose/goal are two spellings of one port, so both need a default too, which means validation can no longer require one of them; on_start() now reports that case by name instead.

action_result is the GetResult response, not the Result. Four nodes read a payload field straight off it and raised on their first live tick:

'ComputePathToPose_GetResult_Response' object has no attribute 'path'

bteng-ros2 documents the property as "Result message from the last completed action" while storing what get_result_async() resolved to -- a wrapper around status and result. Its own code reads action_result.status, which a Result message does not have. bteng_nav2.actions._result.action_result_of() unwraps it, and accepts a bare Result too, so a change on either side of that boundary cannot break the nodes again. Affected: ComputePathToPose, ComputePathThroughPoses, SmoothPath, DockRobot. NavigateToPose and NavigateThroughPoses were accidentally correct -- the field they wanted is itself called result.

--dry-run did not validate. It built each tree and never called validate_tree(), which is what the executor does at construction. The one command whose job is catching a broken tree before the robot could not catch an unbound port at all -- which is how the first defect above shipped. It now validates, and reports each error with the tree and port that produced it.

A literal number in XML arrived as a string, and rclpy aborts the process. <ManageLifecycleNodes command="0"/> handed the node "0"; <Wait wait_duration="3"/>, "3". XML has no types, and every shipped tree and every offline test bound these ports to the blackboard, where the params file had already typed them -- so the literal path was never exercised. Putting a string in a ROS message's numeric field does not raise:

nav2_msgs__srv__manage_lifecycle_nodes__request__convert_from_py:
Assertion `PyLong_Check(field)' failed.

That is SIGABRT: a core dump mid-run, with no summary, no exit code and nothing for a supervisor to act on. 05_full_autonomy.xml did exactly that. xml_integration.coerce_literal_params() now gives every literal the type its port declares, once for all 38 node types, and a value that will not convert raises during --dry-run naming the node and port instead of reaching a robot.

A required numeric port had no default to infer a type from. The coercion above reads the type from the port's declared default, and a required port has none: <DriveOnHeading dist_to_travel="0.5" speed="0.1"/> still aborted, this time in geometry_msgs__msg__point__convert_from_py. Inferring from the literal instead would be worse -- a dock_id of "0123" would silently become an int -- so target_yaw, dist_to_travel, speed and param_value now declare type_hint=float, and the coercion reads that first.

Docking imported a message package that a Nav2 install does not have. No module named 'opennav_docking_msgs' -- docking began in the standalone opennav_docking stack and was merged into Nav2, so Jazzy and newer ship nav2_msgs.action.DockRobot. DockRobotNode and UndockRobotNode now look in nav2_msgs first and fall back to the standalone package, so both kinds of install work. DockRobot.Goal also carries use_dock_id, which defaults to False and makes the server read dock_pose instead: a goal that names a dock by id now says so.

A field that looks like a string but is a message. slam_toolbox declares SaveMap.Request.name as std_msgs/String -- a message -- while SerializePoseGraph.Request.filename, in the same package, is a plain string. SaveSlamMapNode assigned a str to the first, which aborts the process:

std_msgs__msg__string__convert_from_py:
Assertion `strncmp("std_msgs.msg._string.String", ...) == 0' failed.

The test that covered it asserted req.name == "my_map" against a MagicMock -- the very shape that crashes.

None of these was visible offline for the same reason: a MagicMock answers to every attribute name, so a test fixture cannot tell the difference between the object a node expects and the one ROS hands it. The tests added with these fixes use the real message shapes, and each fix was checked by re-introducing the bug.

docs.title: Fixed: seven endpoints that do not exist on a real Nav2 stack
docs.text:
Verified against ros-navigation/navigation2 (main). Every one of these nodes would have failed against any real stack, whatever the discovery logic did — and no stub test could show it, because the fakes answer to whatever name they are handed.

Node Was Now ClearGlobalCostmapNode /clear_costmap_global_srv /global_costmap/clear_entirely_global_costmap ClearLocalCostmapNode /clear_costmap_local_srv /local_costmap/clear_entirely_local_costmap ClearGlobalCostmapAroundRobotNode /clear_global_costmap_around_robot /global_costmap/clear_around_global_costmap ClearLocalCostmapAroundRobotNode /clear_local_costmap_around_robot /local_costmap/clear_around_local_costmap GetGlobalCostmapNode /get_costmap_global /global_costmap/get_costmap GetLocalCostmapNode /get_costmap_local /local_costmap/get_costmap BackUpNode /back_up /backup

Sources: nav2_costmap_2d/src/clear_costmap_service.cpp builds each service as "clear_entirely_"/"clear_around_" + the costmap's name, advertised inside that costmap node's namespace; nav2_bt_navigator's default behaviour tree uses global_costmap/clear_entirely_global_costmap; nav2_bringup/params/nav2_params.yaml registers the reverse behaviour as backup.

ClearGlobalCostmap opens the recovery branch of nearly every Nav2 tree, so recovery would have failed on the first real run.

The corrected names are pinned by a test that cites the Nav2 files they came from, so a future edit cannot quietly undo them. Any of them can still be overridden per-node from XML via the endpoint port added in 0.2.2.

docs.title: Every node can be retargeted from XML
docs.text:
Via bteng-ros2 0.2.3, which declares the endpoint as an input port on the base classes, all 38 nodes here inherit it:

<ComputePathToPose name="plan_a" action_name="/planner_a/compute_path_to_pose" .../>
<IsObstacleNear    name="rear"   topic_name="/scan_rear" min_distance="0.4"/>

Two planners on one robot, a second controller server, or a per-robot namespace were previously impossible to express in a tree — every node pinned its endpoint as a class attribute and only ManageLifecycleNodes had a port for it. The default is still the class attribute, so existing trees are unaffected.

Limitations bteng_nav2_test reported, now closed. No behaviour that worked before changes.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• run_trees(..., manage_context=False) runs in the caller's ROS context instead of calling rclpy.init()/shutdown(), so a supervisor that already owns a context can run a tree without having its own torn down afterwards.
  • make_ros_node(cfg) is public — it is the only thing that applies ros.namespace and use_sim_time to the shared node, and callers were reaching for the private name. The old _make_ros_node still works.
  • ComputePathToPoseNode accepts goal_pose as well as goal. NavigateToPose spells it goal_pose; wiring the two together meant remembering which node used which. goal_pose wins when both are set.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• --namespace silently missed any endpoint bound to a blackboard key. The name lives in the blackboard, and apply_namespace() only rewrote nodes and their params, so service_name="{svc}" escaped the rewrite while every other node was namespaced. It now rewrites the value under the key too, once, idempotently.
  • The executor node did not inherit use_sim_time, so its tick timer ran on the system clock in a sim-time run while the tree nodes followed the sim clock.
Everything here was found by building bteng_nav2_test, a validation project that contains no application Python — the first consumer to use this package the way its README claims it can be used.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• SetInitialPoseNode and PublishGoalPoseNode published into the void. Both created their publisher and published in the same tick. DDS has not matched a subscriber that early, so the message was dropped with no error while the node reported SUCCESS — an initial pose AMCL never receives is the difference between a robot that localizes and one that does not. Both now report RUNNING until a subscriber is matched, publish once, then SUCCESS (match_timeout, default 2 s, then publish anyway; 0 restores the old behaviour). Publishing is now once per activation rather than once per tick.
  • Seven condition classes declared their defaults in the wrong argument. InputPort("low_threshold", "0.20") puts "0.20" in the description slot, so port.default stayed None, the XML parser's default-seeding never fired and provided_ports() advertised a string as documentation. Eight ports fixed.
  • IsEmergencyStopCondition declared a topic_name port that nothing read. RosConditionNode subscribes to the class attribute, so topic_name="/estop" in XML bound cleanly, passed every structural check and did nothing.
  • --dry-run could not run without ROS, contradicting its own documentation as the CI gate. load_config() built real geometry_msgs objects, so the command died at import on any machine without the message packages. Params are now validated rather than built under --dry-run (unknown keys, yaw/quaternion conflicts, unnormalized quaternions and wrong-length covariances are all still caught), so the gate needs no ROS at all — not a graph, not rclpy, not the message packages.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text: • load_config(path, build_messages=True) — pass False to validate without constructing. Typed keys then hold an UnbuiltMessage describing what would have been built.

docs.title: Known limitations found and not yet fixed
docs.text:
• Every node hard-codes its endpoint as a class attribute; only ManageLifecycleNodesNode exposes it as a port. So two planners on one robot, or a FollowPath against a second controller server, cannot be expressed in XML at all.
  • apply_namespace() cannot namespace an endpoint bound to a blackboard key: it rewrites the attribute and NodeConfig.params, never the blackboard.
  • Decorator numbers cannot come from YAML — <Retry num_attempts="{key}"> is rejected at build time, since BTEng resolves those into constructor arguments before a blackboard exists.
Adds the command-line path: a project can now run Nav2 behaviour trees from a params file and XML, with no application Python.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• bteng-nav2 run trees/ -p params.yaml — ROS lifecycle, tick loop, per-leaf reporting, failure report and exit code. --dry-run builds every tree without creating a ROS context (the CI gate), --namespace rewrites absolute action and service names for multi-robot runs, --bb KEY=VALUE overrides seeded values.
  • bteng-nav2 nodes — lists the 76 XML tags (38 node types, each under its short form and its class name).
  • bteng_nav2.xml_integration — register_nodes(), load_tree(), BTENG_NODES, port_model(). load_tree() seeds the parser's port directions from each class's provided_ports(), so path="{path}" on a node that writes path binds as an output. Without that the value is silently dropped.
  • bteng_nav2.config — params YAML to typed ROS messages: pose, pose_cov, poses, path, point, quaternion, duration. Strict validation: a mapping with no type:, an unknown type, an unknown key or a wrong-length covariance is an error naming the blackboard key.
  • bteng_nav2.runtime — run_trees(), run_one(), build_tree(), apply_namespace(), failures(), install_logging().
  • Example params file and five example trees under examples/.
  • docs/guide/cli.md documents the whole workflow.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• 13 action nodes dropped super().on_start()'s return value, so every one of them reported None on its first tick — which the tree read as a terminal result. All now return super().on_start().
  • Every example and doc page called three APIs that did not exist: Tree(root=...) (metadata is positional #1), RosBTExecutor(..., ros_node=...) and executor.run(). The latter two now exist in bteng-ros2 0.2.x; the first was simply wrong.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text: • Requires bteng >= 0.3.1 and bteng-ros2 >= 0.2.1. The bteng-ros2 floor matters most: it carries the server-discovery wait, without which every service node here fails on its first tick against a real Nav2 stack.

docs.title: Known limitation
docs.text: Never run against a real robot or simulator. The suite stubs rclpy and every message package, so timer behaviour, action-client callbacks, discovery timing and use_sim_time are unverified in practice.

docs.title: Compute and follow
docs.text:
Source file: examples/02_compute_and_follow.py

This example demonstrates the two-step path planning and execution pipeline. ComputePathToPoseNode requests a path from the Nav2 planner and writes it to the blackboard. FollowPathNode reads the same key and executes the path with the Nav2 controller. The two nodes are connected by a SequenceNode with no direct coupling — only the blackboard key "path" links them.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
"""Example 02 – Compute a path then follow it.

Demonstrates a two-step pipeline wired through the blackboard:
  1. ComputePathToPoseNode asks the Nav2 planner for a path and writes it
     to blackboard["path"].
  2. FollowPathNode reads blackboard["path"] and executes it with the
     Nav2 controller.

This pattern is useful when you want to inspect or modify the path between
planning and execution (e.g. validate it with IsPathValidNode first).

Tree structure
--------------
SequenceNode
├── ComputePathToPoseNode  goal -> "goal"  |  path -> "path"
└── FollowPathNode         path <- "path"

Run
---
    python3 examples/02_compute_and_follow.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import rclpy

from geometry_msgs.msg import PoseStamped

from bteng import Blackboard, ExecutorConfig, NodeConfig, SequenceNode, Tree, TreeMetadata
from bteng_ros2 import RosBTExecutor

from bteng_nav2 import ComputePathToPoseNode, FollowPathNode


def make_goal(frame_id: str, x: float, y: float, w: float = 1.0) -> PoseStamped:
    """Build a PoseStamped with a 2-D position and yaw-only quaternion."""
    pose = PoseStamped()
    pose.header.frame_id = frame_id
    pose.pose.position.x = x
    pose.pose.position.y = y
    pose.pose.orientation.w = w
    return pose


def main() -> None:
    rclpy.init()
    executor = None

    try:
        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        # 1. Populate the blackboard
        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        bb = Blackboard()
        bb.set("goal", make_goal("map", x=3.0, y=-1.0))

        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        # 2. Build each node
        #    ComputePathToPoseNode writes its result to blackboard["path"].
        #    FollowPathNode reads blackboard["path"].
        #    Neither takes a ros_node: the executor injects itself below.
        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        compute_config = NodeConfig(
            blackboard=bb,
            input_ports={"goal": "goal"},
            output_ports={"path": "path"},
            # "start" has no usable default, so Tree.validate() wants a value:
            # None means "plan from the robot's current pose".
            params={"start": None},
        )
        compute = ComputePathToPoseNode("compute_path", config=compute_config)

        follow_config = NodeConfig(
            blackboard=bb,
            input_ports={"path": "path"},
        )
        follow = FollowPathNode("follow_path", config=follow_config)

        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        # 3. Wire into a sequence and run
        #    Tree() takes the metadata first, then the root node.
        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        sequence = SequenceNode("pipeline", children=[compute, follow])
        tree = Tree(TreeMetadata(id="compute_and_follow"), sequence)
        executor = RosBTExecutor(tree, ExecutorConfig(tick_interval=0.05))

        executor.get_logger().info("Planning and following path to (3.0, -1.0) …")
        # run() spins until the sequence settles, then returns its status.
        status = executor.run(timeout=120.0)
        executor.get_logger().info(f"Tree finished: {status.value}")

    finally:
        if executor is not None:
            executor.destroy_node()
        rclpy.shutdown()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: Full autonomy
docs.text:
Source file: examples/05_full_autonomy.py

This example demonstrates a production-style tree that handles three real-world concerns before committing to navigation: a localization gate that fails fast when AMCL is not active, a goal proximity check that skips navigation when the robot is already at the destination, and a navigation sequence with a costmap-clear-and-spin recovery branch.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
"""Example 05 – Full autonomy: localization check, goal skip, and recovery.

Demonstrates a production-style tree that handles three common real-world
concerns before committing to navigation:

  1. Localization gate – fail fast if AMCL has not published a pose.
  2. Goal proximity skip – if the robot is already near the goal, succeed
     immediately without sending a navigation goal.
  3. Navigation with recovery – try NavigateToPoseNode; on failure clear
     costmaps and spin before giving up.

Tree structure
--------------
FallbackNode (root)
├── SequenceNode (pre-checks)
│   ├── IsLocalizationActiveCondition   AMCL alive?
│   └── IsRobotNearGoalCondition        already at goal? → SUCCESS skips nav
├── SequenceNode (navigation)
│   ├── IsNavigationActiveCondition     action server ready?
│   └── NavigateToPoseNode              send goal
└── SequenceNode (recovery)
    ├── ClearGlobalCostmapNode          wipe stale obstacles
    └── SpinNode                        reorient for replanning

Evaluation order
----------------
- If AMCL is alive AND the robot is already near the goal, the pre-checks
  sequence returns SUCCESS → the root FallbackNode short-circuits and the
  whole tree succeeds without navigating.
- Otherwise the pre-checks sequence fails (either AMCL is dead, or the
  robot is not near the goal), and the FallbackNode tries the navigation
  sequence.
- If navigation fails, the FallbackNode tries the recovery sequence.

Run
---
    python3 examples/05_full_autonomy.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import rclpy

from geometry_msgs.msg import PoseStamped

from bteng import (
    Blackboard,
    ExecutorConfig,
    FallbackNode,
    NodeConfig,
    NodeStatus,
    SequenceNode,
    Tree,
    TreeMetadata,
)
from bteng_ros2 import RosBTExecutor

from bteng_nav2 import (
    ClearGlobalCostmapNode,
    IsLocalizationActiveCondition,
    IsNavigationActiveCondition,
    IsRobotNearGoalCondition,
    NavigateToPoseNode,
    SpinNode,
)


def make_goal(frame_id: str, x: float, y: float, w: float = 1.0) -> PoseStamped:
    """Build a PoseStamped with a 2-D position and yaw-only quaternion."""
    pose = PoseStamped()
    pose.header.frame_id = frame_id
    pose.pose.position.x = x
    pose.pose.position.y = y
    pose.pose.orientation.w = w
    return pose


def main() -> None:
    rclpy.init()
    executor = None

    try:
        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        # 1. Shared blackboard
        #    No node below takes a ros_node: RosBTExecutor is an rclpy node
        #    and injects itself into every ROS-aware node of the tree.
        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        bb = Blackboard()
        bb.set("goal_pose", make_goal("map", x=5.0, y=3.0))
        bb.set("goal_tolerance", 0.3)   # metres – passed to IsRobotNearGoal
        bb.set("amcl_timeout", 2.0)     # seconds – passed to IsLocalizationActive
        bb.set("target_yaw", 1.57)      # ~90° spin during recovery

        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        # 2. Pre-check sequence: localization alive AND near goal already?
        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        loc_config = NodeConfig(
            blackboard=bb,
            input_ports={"timeout": "amcl_timeout"},
        )
        loc_check = IsLocalizationActiveCondition(
            "localization_active", config=loc_config
        )

        near_goal_config = NodeConfig(
            blackboard=bb,
            input_ports={
                "goal_pose": "goal_pose",
                "tolerance": "goal_tolerance",
            },
        )
        near_goal = IsRobotNearGoalCondition("near_goal", config=near_goal_config)

        pre_checks = SequenceNode("pre_checks", children=[loc_check, near_goal])

        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        # 3. Navigation sequence: server ready, then navigate
        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        nav_active_config = NodeConfig(blackboard=bb)
        nav_active = IsNavigationActiveCondition(
            "nav_active", config=nav_active_config
        )

        navigate_config = NodeConfig(
            blackboard=bb,
            input_ports={"goal_pose": "goal_pose"},
            output_ports={"result": "nav_result"},
        )
        navigate = NavigateToPoseNode("navigate", config=navigate_config)

        nav_sequence = SequenceNode(
            "navigation", children=[nav_active, navigate]
        )

        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        # 4. Recovery sequence: clear costmap then spin
        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        clear_config = NodeConfig(blackboard=bb)
        clear = ClearGlobalCostmapNode("clear_costmap", config=clear_config)

        spin_config = NodeConfig(
            blackboard=bb,
            input_ports={"target_yaw": "target_yaw"},
        )
        spin = SpinNode("spin", config=spin_config)

        recovery_sequence = SequenceNode(
            "recovery", children=[clear, spin]
        )

        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        # 5. Root fallback: pre-checks | navigation | recovery
        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        root = FallbackNode(
            "root",
            children=[pre_checks, nav_sequence, recovery_sequence],
        )

        tree = Tree(TreeMetadata(id="full_autonomy"), root)
        executor = RosBTExecutor(tree, ExecutorConfig(tick_interval=0.05))

        executor.get_logger().info("Running full-autonomy tree …")
        # run() spins until the root settles and returns that status; on
        # timeout it halts the tree and returns FAILURE.
        status = executor.run(timeout=180.0)

        if status == NodeStatus.SUCCESS:
            executor.get_logger().info("Tree succeeded.")
        else:
            executor.get_logger().error("Tree failed – manual intervention required.")

    finally:
        if executor is not None:
            executor.destroy_node()
        rclpy.shutdown()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: Navigate to pose
docs.text:
Source file: examples/01_navigate_to_pose.py

This example shows the simplest possible bteng-nav2 tree: a single NavigateToPoseNode that sends one goal to the Nav2 stack and blocks until navigation succeeds or fails. It demonstrates how to construct a goal pose, wire it through the blackboard, and run the tree with RosBTExecutor.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
"""Example 01 – Navigate to a fixed goal pose.

Demonstrates the simplest possible bteng_nav2 tree: a single
NavigateToPoseNode that sends one goal to the Nav2 stack and blocks
until navigation succeeds or fails.

Tree structure
--------------
NavigateToPoseNode
    input:  goal_pose  <- blackboard["goal_pose"]
    output: result     -> blackboard["nav_result"]

Run
---
    python3 examples/01_navigate_to_pose.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import rclpy

from geometry_msgs.msg import PoseStamped

from bteng import Blackboard, ExecutorConfig, NodeConfig, Tree, TreeMetadata
from bteng_ros2 import RosBTExecutor

from bteng_nav2 import NavigateToPoseNode


def make_goal(frame_id: str, x: float, y: float, w: float = 1.0) -> PoseStamped:
    """Build a PoseStamped with a 2-D position and yaw-only quaternion."""
    pose = PoseStamped()
    pose.header.frame_id = frame_id
    pose.pose.position.x = x
    pose.pose.position.y = y
    pose.pose.orientation.w = w
    return pose


def main() -> None:
    rclpy.init()
    executor = None

    try:
        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        # 1. Populate the blackboard
        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        bb = Blackboard()
        bb.set("goal_pose", make_goal("map", x=2.0, y=1.5))

        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        # 2. Build the node
        #    No ros_node here: RosBTExecutor is itself an rclpy node and
        #    injects itself into every ROS-aware node of the tree.
        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        config = NodeConfig(
            blackboard=bb,
            input_ports={"goal_pose": "goal_pose"},
            output_ports={"result": "nav_result"},
        )
        navigate = NavigateToPoseNode("navigate", config=config)

        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        # 3. Wrap in a tree and run
        #    Tree() takes the metadata first, then the root node.
        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        tree = Tree(TreeMetadata(id="navigate_to_pose"), navigate)
        executor = RosBTExecutor(tree, ExecutorConfig(tick_interval=0.05))

        executor.get_logger().info("Navigating to (2.0, 1.5) …")
        # run() spins until the root reports SUCCESS/FAILURE; the ticking
        # itself comes from the timer the executor created.
        status = executor.run(timeout=120.0)
        executor.get_logger().info(f"Tree finished: {status.value}")

    finally:
        if executor is not None:
            executor.destroy_node()
        rclpy.shutdown()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: How to run
docs.text:
With ROS 2 sourced and a Nav2 stack running:

source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
python3 examples/01_navigate_to_pose.py

The script logs Navigating to (2.0, 1.5) when the action is sent and Tree finished: SUCCESS (or FAILURE) when NavigateToPoseNode settles. run(timeout=120.0) bounds the wait: on expiry the tree is halted and FAILURE is returned rather than hanging forever.

The same tree needs no Python at all — see Running from the CLI:

bteng-nav2 run examples/trees/01_navigate_to_pose.xml -p examples/config/nav2_params.yaml

docs.title: Patrol loop
docs.text:
Source file: examples/03_patrol_loop.py

This example demonstrates continuous patrol behaviour. The robot cycles through a fixed list of waypoints indefinitely using NavigateThroughPosesNode. The waypoint list is refreshed on the blackboard before each tree run so the node always navigates the full route from the beginning. Send SIGINT (Ctrl-C) to stop the loop cleanly.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
"""Example 03 – Patrol loop through a list of waypoints.

Demonstrates continuous patrol behaviour: the robot cycles through a fixed
list of waypoints indefinitely using NavigateThroughPosesNode.  A new set
of poses is written to the blackboard before each tree tick, so the node
always navigates the full route.

To stop the loop send SIGINT (Ctrl-C).

Tree structure
--------------
NavigateThroughPosesNode   poses <- "waypoints"

The tree is re-run in an infinite loop after each successful lap so the
robot keeps patrolling until the user interrupts the process.  A settled
tree has its tick timer cancelled, so every lap gets a fresh executor —
re-calling run() on the old one would only return the recorded status.

Run
---
    python3 examples/03_patrol_loop.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import signal
import sys

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node

from geometry_msgs.msg import PoseStamped

from bteng import Blackboard, ExecutorConfig, NodeConfig, Tree, TreeMetadata
from bteng_ros2 import RosBTExecutor

from bteng_nav2 import NavigateThroughPosesNode


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Helpers
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def make_pose(frame_id: str, x: float, y: float, w: float = 1.0) -> PoseStamped:
    """Build a PoseStamped with a 2-D position and yaw-only quaternion."""
    pose = PoseStamped()
    pose.header.frame_id = frame_id
    pose.pose.position.x = x
    pose.pose.position.y = y
    pose.pose.orientation.w = w
    return pose


def build_waypoints(frame_id: str = "map") -> list[PoseStamped]:
    """Return the patrol route as an ordered list of PoseStamped messages."""
    return [
        make_pose(frame_id, x=0.0,  y=0.0),
        make_pose(frame_id, x=3.0,  y=0.0),
        make_pose(frame_id, x=3.0,  y=3.0),
        make_pose(frame_id, x=0.0,  y=3.0),
    ]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Main
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def main() -> None:
    rclpy.init()
    # This example owns its node instead of letting the executor be the node:
    # the tree node outlives every per-lap executor, so its action client must
    # be bound to a node that stays alive for the whole patrol.
    ros_node = Node("bteng_patrol_loop")

    # Graceful shutdown on Ctrl-C
    running = [True]

    def _sigint_handler(sig, frame):
        ros_node.get_logger().info("Patrol interrupted – shutting down.")
        running[0] = False

    signal.signal(signal.SIGINT, _sigint_handler)

    try:
        bb = Blackboard()
        waypoints = build_waypoints()
        bb.set("waypoints", waypoints)

        config = NodeConfig(
            blackboard=bb,
            input_ports={"poses": "waypoints"},
            output_ports={"result": "patrol_result"},
        )
        navigate = NavigateThroughPosesNode(
            "patrol", config=config, ros_node=ros_node
        )

        tree = Tree(TreeMetadata(id="patrol_loop"), navigate)

        lap = 0
        while running[0]:
            lap += 1
            ros_node.get_logger().info(f"Starting patrol lap {lap} …")

            # Refresh waypoints on the blackboard before each run so that
            # timestamps or dynamic changes can be applied here.
            bb.set("waypoints", waypoints)

            # One executor per lap: once a tree settles its tick timer is
            # cancelled, so run() on the previous executor would return the
            # recorded status without sending a new goal.  The tree node keeps
            # ros_node, which the executor spins alongside its own node.
            executor = RosBTExecutor(
                tree,
                ExecutorConfig(tick_interval=0.05),
                node_name=f"patrol_ticker_{lap}",
                ros_node=ros_node,
            )
            try:
                status = executor.run(timeout=300.0)
            finally:
                executor.destroy_node()

            if not running[0]:
                break
            ros_node.get_logger().info(
                f"Lap {lap} complete ({status.value}) – restarting."
            )

    finally:
        ros_node.destroy_node()
        rclpy.shutdown()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: How to run
docs.text:
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
python3 examples/03_patrol_loop.py

The script logs Starting patrol lap N at the start of each lap and Lap N complete after each successful circuit. Press Ctrl-C to exit cleanly.

To change the patrol route, modify the build_waypoints() function or update bb.set("waypoints", ...) inside the loop before the lap's run().

Each lap builds a new RosBTExecutor. Once a tree settles, its tick timer is cancelled, so calling run() again on the same executor returns the recorded status without sending a fresh goal. The tree node keeps the long-lived ros_node, which the per-lap executor spins alongside its own node.

For a fixed route and no looping, the same job is one command with no Python:

bteng-nav2 run examples/trees/03_waypoints.xml -p examples/config/nav2_params.yaml

docs.title: Recovery tree
docs.text:
Source file: examples/04_recovery_tree.py

This example demonstrates a robust navigation tree that attempts a primary NavigateToPoseNode and, on failure, runs a recovery sequence before retrying. The recovery sequence clears stale costmap data, backs the robot away from the obstacle, and spins to reorient before sending the goal again. If the retry also fails the tree returns FAILURE.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
"""Example 04 – Navigation with recovery fallback.

Demonstrates a robust navigation tree that attempts the primary
NavigateToPoseNode and, on failure, runs a recovery sequence before
retrying navigation.

Tree structure
--------------
FallbackNode                          (try primary first)
├── NavigateToPoseNode (primary)      goal_pose <- "goal_pose"
└── SequenceNode (recovery + retry)
    ├── ClearGlobalCostmapNode        clear stale obstacles
    ├── BackUpNode                    move away from obstacle
    ├── SpinNode                      reorient to find new path
    └── NavigateToPoseNode (retry)    goal_pose <- "goal_pose"

If the retry also fails the FallbackNode returns FAILURE and the program
reports that navigation could not be completed.

Run
---
    python3 examples/04_recovery_tree.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import rclpy

from geometry_msgs.msg import PoseStamped

from bteng import (
    Blackboard,
    ExecutorConfig,
    NodeConfig,
    FallbackNode,
    SequenceNode,
    Tree,
    TreeMetadata,
    NodeStatus,
)
from bteng_ros2 import RosBTExecutor

from bteng_nav2 import (
    NavigateToPoseNode,
    ClearGlobalCostmapNode,
    BackUpNode,
    SpinNode,
)


def make_goal(frame_id: str, x: float, y: float, w: float = 1.0) -> PoseStamped:
    """Build a PoseStamped with a 2-D position and yaw-only quaternion."""
    pose = PoseStamped()
    pose.header.frame_id = frame_id
    pose.pose.position.x = x
    pose.pose.position.y = y
    pose.pose.orientation.w = w
    return pose


def main() -> None:
    rclpy.init()
    executor = None

    try:
        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        # 1. Shared blackboard: both navigate nodes read the same goal
        #    None of the nodes below takes a ros_node — RosBTExecutor is an
        #    rclpy node and injects itself into all of them.
        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        bb = Blackboard()
        bb.set("goal_pose", make_goal("map", x=4.0, y=2.0))
        bb.set("backup_dist", 0.3)
        bb.set("target_yaw", 1.57)   # ~90 degrees

        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        # 2. Primary navigation attempt
        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        primary_config = NodeConfig(
            blackboard=bb,
            input_ports={"goal_pose": "goal_pose"},
            output_ports={"result": "nav_result"},
        )
        primary_nav = NavigateToPoseNode("primary_nav", config=primary_config)

        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        # 3. Recovery sequence
        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        clear_config = NodeConfig(blackboard=bb)
        clear = ClearGlobalCostmapNode("clear_costmap", config=clear_config)

        backup_config = NodeConfig(
            blackboard=bb,
            input_ports={"backup_dist": "backup_dist"},
        )
        backup = BackUpNode("back_up", config=backup_config)

        spin_config = NodeConfig(
            blackboard=bb,
            input_ports={"target_yaw": "target_yaw"},
        )
        spin = SpinNode("spin", config=spin_config)

        retry_config = NodeConfig(
            blackboard=bb,
            input_ports={"goal_pose": "goal_pose"},
            output_ports={"result": "retry_result"},
        )
        retry_nav = NavigateToPoseNode("retry_nav", config=retry_config)

        recovery_seq = SequenceNode(
            "recovery",
            children=[clear, backup, spin, retry_nav],
        )

        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        # 4. Top-level fallback
        # ------------------------------------------------------------------
        root = FallbackNode("root", children=[primary_nav, recovery_seq])
        tree = Tree(TreeMetadata(id="recovery_tree"), root)
        executor = RosBTExecutor(tree, ExecutorConfig(tick_interval=0.05))

        executor.get_logger().info("Navigating to (4.0, 2.0) with recovery …")
        # run() returns the status the root settled at — FAILURE also if the
        # timeout expires, in which case the tree is halted first.
        status = executor.run(timeout=180.0)

        if status == NodeStatus.SUCCESS:
            executor.get_logger().info("Navigation succeeded.")
        else:
            executor.get_logger().error("Navigation failed after recovery.")

    finally:
        if executor is not None:
            executor.destroy_node()
        rclpy.shutdown()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.text:
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash

The tree logs whether navigation ultimately succeeded or failed after the recovery attempt. Adjust backup_dist and target_yaw on the blackboard to tune the recovery behaviour for your robot.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: bteng-nav2 requires Python 3.10 or newer and a sourced ROS 2 Humble, Iron, or Jazzy workspace.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Install and source ROS 2 before installing bteng-nav2. The package imports rclpy, nav2_msgs, and other ROS 2 Python packages at runtime, so those must be on your PYTHONPATH.

# Humble example — adjust the distro name as needed
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash

Verify the ROS environment is active:

python3 -c "import rclpy; print('rclpy ok')"

docs.title: Standard install
docs.text:
With ROS 2 sourced:

pip install bteng-nav2

This pulls in bteng >= 0.3.1 and bteng-ros2 >= 0.2.3. Both pins are load-bearing rather than cosmetic: bteng-ros2 0.2.3 provides RosBTExecutor.run(), its ros_node= argument, the server-discovery wait every service node needs on a real graph, and the endpoint ports described in Retargeting endpoints.

Verify the install:

python3 -c "import bteng_nav2; print(bteng_nav2.__version__)"
bteng-nav2 nodes | head            # the CLI is installed as an entry point

docs.title: Virtual environment (recommended)
docs.text:
Use a virtual environment to avoid polluting the system Python. When creating the environment, pass --system-site-packages so that rclpy and the ROS 2 message packages remain accessible:

python3 -m venv --system-site-packages .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

pip install bteng-nav2

docs.title: Development install (from source)
docs.text:
If you are contributing to bteng-nav2 or want to run the test suite:

git clone https://github.com/mdirzpr/BTEng_nav2.git
cd BTEng_nav2
python3 -m venv --system-site-packages .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

pip install -e ".[dev]"
pytest -q

The -e flag installs in editable mode — changes to the source are reflected immediately without reinstalling.

docs.title: Running tests
docs.text:
The test suite runs without a live ROS 2 instance. The bundled conftest.py stubs all ROS 2 message and service types.

# Full test suite
pytest tests/ -v

# Individual files
pytest tests/test_actions.py
pytest tests/test_services.py
pytest tests/test_conditions.py

All tests should pass with or without ROS 2 installed.

docs.text:
Problem Fix ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'rclpy' Source your ROS 2 workspace: source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'bteng_nav2' Activate the virtual environment: source .venv/bin/activate ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'nav2_msgs' Install the Nav2 packages for your distro: sudo apt install ros-humble-nav2-msgs Old version after pip install Run pip install --upgrade bteng-nav2

Next: Quick Start.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text: There are two ways to send a navigation goal with bteng-nav2. Start with the first one — most projects never need the second.

docs.title: Without writing Python
docs.text:
Two files and a command. params.yaml holds the values, the tree holds the behaviour:

# params.yaml
ros:
  namespace: ""
  use_sim_time: false
blackboard:
  goal_pose: {type: pose, frame_id: map, x: 2.0, y: 1.5, yaw: 0.0}

<!-- trees/navigate.xml -->
<BTEng format_version="1.0" main_tree_to_execute="main">
  <Tree ID="main">
    <NavigateToPose name="go" goal_pose="{goal_pose}" result="{nav_result}" />
  </Tree>
</BTEng>

bteng-nav2 run trees/navigate.xml -p params.yaml --dry-run   # builds it, no ROS needed
bteng-nav2 run trees/navigate.xml -p params.yaml             # runs it

Poses are built in YAML because an XML attribute is a string and NavigateToPose wants a geometry_msgs/PoseStamped; the params loader has typed builders for poses, paths, points, quaternions and durations. Exit code is 0 only if every tree succeeded, so this drops straight into CI. See Running from the CLI.

docs.title: From Python
docs.text: The rest of this page is the same goal built by hand — for embedding a tree in a larger application, or mixing these nodes with your own. The full example is at examples/01_navigate_to_pose.py.

docs.title: 1. Build a goal pose
docs.text:
from geometry_msgs.msg import PoseStamped

def make_goal(frame_id: str, x: float, y: float, w: float = 1.0) -> PoseStamped:
    pose = PoseStamped()
    pose.header.frame_id = frame_id
    pose.pose.position.x = x
    pose.pose.position.y = y
    pose.pose.orientation.w = w
    return pose

docs.title: 2. Populate the blackboard
docs.text:
from bteng import Blackboard

bb = Blackboard()
bb.set("goal_pose", make_goal("map", x=2.0, y=1.5))

docs.title: 3. Create the node
docs.text:
from bteng import NodeConfig
from bteng_nav2 import NavigateToPoseNode

config = NodeConfig(
    blackboard=bb,
    input_ports={"goal_pose": "goal_pose"},
    output_ports={"result": "nav_result"},
)
navigate = NavigateToPoseNode("navigate", config=config)

input_ports maps the node's port name to the blackboard key that holds the value. output_ports maps the node's output port name to the key where the result is written.

No ros_node= is needed here: the executor injects one at set_tree() time (step 4). Pass it at construction only when the node must use a specific rclpy.Node.

docs.title: 4. Run with RosBTExecutor
docs.text:
import rclpy
from bteng import ExecutorConfig, Tree, TreeMetadata
from bteng_ros2 import RosBTExecutor

rclpy.init()
executor = None

try:
    bb = Blackboard()
    bb.set("goal_pose", make_goal("map", x=2.0, y=1.5))

    config = NodeConfig(
        blackboard=bb,
        input_ports={"goal_pose": "goal_pose"},
        output_ports={"result": "nav_result"},
    )
    navigate = NavigateToPoseNode("navigate", config=config)

    tree = Tree(TreeMetadata(id="quickstart"), navigate)
    executor = RosBTExecutor(tree, ExecutorConfig(tick_interval=0.05))
    status = executor.run(timeout=120.0)
finally:
    if executor is not None:
        executor.destroy_node()
    rclpy.shutdown()

Tree takes its metadata first and the root node second. RosBTExecutor is itself an rclpy.Node and injects itself into every ROS-aware node in the tree, so the nodes need no ros_node=; pass ros_node= only when you want the tree to share a node you already own.

run(timeout=None) spins until the root returns SUCCESS or FAILURE and returns that status. The ticking comes from the timer the executor created in its constructor — run() only spins, so callbacks from action and service clients are served while the tree waits. On timeout the tree is halted and FAILURE is returned. rclpy.init() and rclpy.shutdown() remain the caller's job.

docs.title: 5. Or skip the Python entirely
docs.text:
The same goal, as a params file plus a tree, run with one command:

bteng-nav2 run trees/ -p params.yaml

See Running from the CLI.

docs.title: What happened
docs.text: NavigateToPoseNode is a RosActionNode. On the first tick it reads goal_pose from the blackboard, constructs a NavigateToPose.Goal, and sends it to the /navigate_to_pose action server. On each subsequent tick it checks the action status. When the action server reports success, the node writes the action result to nav_result on the blackboard and returns NodeStatus.SUCCESS.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
Mistake Fix Forgetting to source ROS 2 before running source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash Passing a PoseStamped with an empty frame_id Always set pose.header.frame_id — Nav2 requires a valid TF frame No Nav2 stack running Start Nav2 before executing the tree; the action server must be available Tree(root=node) Tree takes metadata first: Tree(TreeMetadata(id="…"), node) Building a node outside a tree the executor drives Every bteng-nav2 node needs a live rclpy.node.Node; RosBTExecutor injects one, otherwise pass ros_node= yourself rclpy.spin(bt) for a one-shot tree It never returns after the tree settles — use bt.run(timeout=…)

Next: Action Nodes.

docs.title: Action nodes
docs.text:
Action nodes wrap Nav2 ROS 2 action clients. Each node sends a goal to an action server, returns RUNNING while the action is in progress, and returns SUCCESS or FAILURE when the action server responds.

All action nodes inherit from RosActionNode. A ros_node is not required at construction: RosBTExecutor injects itself into every ROS-aware node in the tree when it starts, which is why a tree built from XML by bteng-nav2 run needs no ROS handle anywhere. Pass ros_node= yourself only when you want the node to use a handle other than the executor's.

Every action node's server is settable per node — see Retargeting endpoints:

<ComputePathToPose name="plan_b" goal="{goal}" path="{path_b}"
                   action_name="/planner_b/compute_path_to_pose" />

docs.title: NavigateToPoseNode
docs.text:
Send a single goal pose to the /navigate_to_pose action server. The Nav2 stack handles global planning, local control, and recovery internally.

Ports

Name Direction Default Description goal_pose IN — PoseStamped target pose in the map frame behavior_tree IN "" Path to an XML behavior tree override; empty uses the Nav2 default result OUT — NavigateToPose.Result written on success

Example

from bteng import Blackboard, NodeConfig, Tree, TreeMetadata
from bteng_ros2 import RosBTExecutor
from bteng_nav2 import NavigateToPoseNode

bb = Blackboard()
bb.set("goal_pose", make_goal("map", x=2.0, y=1.5))

config = NodeConfig(
    blackboard=bb,
    input_ports={"goal_pose": "goal_pose"},
    output_ports={"result": "nav_result"},
)
node = NavigateToPoseNode("navigate", config=config, ros_node=ros_node)
executor = RosBTExecutor(Tree(TreeMetadata(id="navigate"), node), ros_node=ros_node)
status = executor.run(timeout=120.0)

docs.title: NavigateThroughPosesNode
docs.text:
Send an ordered list of PoseStamped waypoints to the /navigate_through_poses action server. The robot visits each pose in order.

Ports

Name Direction Default Description poses IN — list[PoseStamped] ordered waypoints behavior_tree IN "" Behavior tree override path result OUT — NavigateThroughPoses.Result written on success

Example

from bteng_nav2 import NavigateThroughPosesNode

bb.set("waypoints", [make_goal("map", 0.0, 0.0), make_goal("map", 3.0, 0.0)])

config = NodeConfig(
    blackboard=bb,
    input_ports={"poses": "waypoints"},
    output_ports={"result": "patrol_result"},
)
node = NavigateThroughPosesNode("patrol", config=config, ros_node=ros_node)

docs.title: ComputePathToPoseNode
docs.text:
Request a path to a single goal from the Nav2 planner server (/compute_path_to_pose). The resulting nav_msgs/Path is written to the blackboard for use by FollowPathNode or IsPathValidNode.

Ports

Name Direction Default Description goal IN — PoseStamped target pose start IN None Optional PoseStamped start pose; omit to use the robot's current pose planner_id IN "" Planner plugin identifier path OUT — nav_msgs/Path computed path

Example

from bteng_nav2 import ComputePathToPoseNode

bb.set("goal", make_goal("map", x=3.0, y=-1.0))

config = NodeConfig(
    blackboard=bb,
    input_ports={"goal": "goal"},
    output_ports={"path": "path"},
)
node = ComputePathToPoseNode("compute", config=config, ros_node=ros_node)

docs.title: ComputePathThroughPosesNode
docs.text:
Request a path through multiple waypoints from the Nav2 planner server (/compute_path_through_poses).

Ports

Name Direction Default Description goals IN — list[PoseStamped] ordered waypoints start IN None Optional start pose planner_id IN "" Planner plugin identifier path OUT — nav_msgs/Path computed path

docs.title: FollowPathNode
docs.text:
Execute a pre-computed path with the Nav2 controller server (/follow_path). Pair with ComputePathToPoseNode via a shared blackboard key.

Ports

Name Direction Default Description path IN — nav_msgs/Path to follow controller_id IN "" Controller plugin identifier goal_checker_id IN "" Goal checker plugin identifier

Example

from bteng import SequenceNode, Tree
from bteng_nav2 import ComputePathToPoseNode, FollowPathNode

compute_config = NodeConfig(
    blackboard=bb,
    input_ports={"goal": "goal"},
    output_ports={"path": "path"},
)
compute = ComputePathToPoseNode("compute", config=compute_config, ros_node=ros_node)

follow_config = NodeConfig(
    blackboard=bb,
    input_ports={"path": "path"},
)
follow = FollowPathNode("follow", config=follow_config, ros_node=ros_node)

sequence = SequenceNode("pipeline", children=[compute, follow])

docs.title: SmoothPathNode
docs.text:
Smooth a path with the Nav2 smoother server (/smooth_path) before following it.

Ports

Name Direction Default Description path IN — nav_msgs/Path to smooth smoother_id IN "" Smoother plugin identifier max_smoothing_duration IN 10.0 Maximum time budget in seconds smoothed_path OUT — nav_msgs/Path smoothed result

docs.title: SpinNode
docs.text:
Rotate the robot in place by target_yaw radians (/spin). Use as a recovery behaviour after a navigation failure to allow the planner to find a new path.

Ports

Name Direction Default Description target_yaw IN — Rotation angle in radians time_allowance IN 10.0 Time limit in seconds

Example

from bteng_nav2 import SpinNode

bb.set("target_yaw", 1.57)  # 90 degrees

config = NodeConfig(
    blackboard=bb,
    input_ports={"target_yaw": "target_yaw"},
)
spin = SpinNode("spin", config=config, ros_node=ros_node)

docs.title: BackUpNode
docs.text:
Drive the robot straight back by backup_dist metres at backup_speed m/s (/backup).

Ports

Name Direction Default Description backup_dist IN 0.15 Distance to reverse in metres backup_speed IN 0.025 Speed in m/s time_allowance IN 10.0 Time limit in seconds

docs.title: DriveOnHeadingNode
docs.text:
Drive forward along the robot's current heading by dist_to_travel metres (/drive_on_heading).

Ports

Name Direction Default Description dist_to_travel IN — Distance to drive in metres speed IN — Forward speed in m/s time_allowance IN 10.0 Time limit in seconds

docs.title: WaitNode
docs.text:

docs.title: AssistedTeleopNode

docs.title: DockRobotNode
docs.text:

Example

from bteng_nav2 import DockRobotNode

bb.set("dock_id", "charger_dock")

config = NodeConfig(
    blackboard=bb,
    input_ports={"dock_id": "dock_id"},
