docs.title: Building trees
docs.text: bteng-nav2 nodes are standard bteng nodes. They compose with SequenceNode, FallbackNode, ParallelNode, decorators, and any custom nodes you write. This page shows the most common patterns.

docs.title: Sequence: compute then follow
docs.text:
The compute-and-follow pipeline is the lowest-level navigation pattern. ComputePathToPoseNode writes a path to the blackboard; FollowPathNode reads it. Both nodes share the same blackboard.

from bteng import Blackboard, ExecutorConfig, NodeConfig, SequenceNode, Tree, TreeMetadata
from bteng_ros2 import RosBTExecutor
from bteng_nav2 import ComputePathToPoseNode, FollowPathNode

bb = Blackboard()
bb.set("goal", make_goal("map", x=3.0, y=-1.0))

compute_config = NodeConfig(
    blackboard=bb,
    input_ports={"goal": "goal"},
    output_ports={"path": "path"},   # writes to bb["path"]
)
compute = ComputePathToPoseNode("compute", config=compute_config, ros_node=ros_node)

follow_config = NodeConfig(
    blackboard=bb,
    input_ports={"path": "path"},    # reads from bb["path"]
)
follow = FollowPathNode("follow", config=follow_config, ros_node=ros_node)

sequence = SequenceNode("pipeline", children=[compute, follow])
tree = Tree(TreeMetadata(id="compute_and_follow"), sequence)
executor = RosBTExecutor(tree, ExecutorConfig(tick_interval=0.05), ros_node=ros_node)
status = executor.run(timeout=120.0)

The SequenceNode ticks compute first. If the planner returns a path the node writes it to bb["path"] and returns SUCCESS. The sequence then ticks follow, which reads the same key. If either child fails the sequence stops immediately.

docs.title: FallbackNode: navigate with recovery
docs.text:
A FallbackNode tries its children in order and returns SUCCESS as soon as one succeeds. Use it to wrap a primary navigation attempt with a recovery sequence.

from bteng import FallbackNode, SequenceNode, NodeConfig, Tree
from bteng_nav2 import NavigateToPoseNode, ClearGlobalCostmapNode, BackUpNode, SpinNode

primary_config = NodeConfig(
    blackboard=bb,
    input_ports={"goal_pose": "goal_pose"},
    output_ports={"result": "nav_result"},
)
primary = NavigateToPoseNode("primary", config=primary_config, ros_node=ros_node)

clear_config = NodeConfig(blackboard=bb)
clear = ClearGlobalCostmapNode("clear", config=clear_config, ros_node=ros_node)

backup_config = NodeConfig(
    blackboard=bb,
    input_ports={"backup_dist": "backup_dist"},
)
backup = BackUpNode("backup", config=backup_config, ros_node=ros_node)

spin_config = NodeConfig(
    blackboard=bb,
    input_ports={"target_yaw": "target_yaw"},
)
spin = SpinNode("spin", config=spin_config, ros_node=ros_node)

retry_config = NodeConfig(
    blackboard=bb,
    input_ports={"goal_pose": "goal_pose"},
    output_ports={"result": "retry_result"},
)
retry = NavigateToPoseNode("retry", config=retry_config, ros_node=ros_node)

recovery = SequenceNode("recovery", children=[clear, backup, spin, retry])
root = FallbackNode("root", children=[primary, recovery])
tree = Tree(TreeMetadata(id="navigate_with_recovery"), root)

Execution flow:

  1. Tick primary. If it returns SUCCESS, the fallback returns SUCCESS and recovery is never run.
  2. If primary returns FAILURE, the fallback ticks recovery.
  3. recovery runs clear, backup, spin, then retry in order.
  4. If retry succeeds, the sequence returns SUCCESS and the fallback returns SUCCESS.
  5. If retry also fails, the fallback returns FAILURE.

docs.title: Blackboard wiring between nodes
docs.text:
Every input port maps a port name to a blackboard key. Every output port maps a port name to the key where the result is written. Two nodes share data by reading and writing the same key.

# Node A writes "path"
config_a = NodeConfig(
    blackboard=bb,
    output_ports={"path": "shared_path"},
)

# Node B reads the same key
config_b = NodeConfig(
    blackboard=bb,
    input_ports={"path": "shared_path"},
)

There is no explicit wiring step. The blackboard is the shared state. You can inspect any key at runtime with bb.get("shared_path") for debugging.

docs.title: Passing ros_node via RosBTExecutor
docs.text:
Every bteng-nav2 node that calls a ROS 2 service or action requires a live rclpy.node.Node. Pass it at construction time:

import rclpy
from rclpy.node import Node

rclpy.init()
ros_node = Node("my_bt_node")

navigate = NavigateToPoseNode("navigate", config=config, ros_node=ros_node)

Pass that same node to RosBTExecutor as ros_node=, so it is spun alongside the executor's own node and its client callbacks are delivered:

from bteng import ExecutorConfig, TreeMetadata
from bteng_ros2 import RosBTExecutor

tree = Tree(TreeMetadata(id="navigate"), navigate)
executor = RosBTExecutor(tree, ExecutorConfig(tick_interval=0.05), ros_node=ros_node)
status = executor.run(timeout=120.0)

Use a single ros_node instance across all nodes in one tree. Sharing the node lets the action and service clients share one executor and callback group without conflicts.

If you have no reason to own a node, drop ros_node= entirely: RosBTExecutor is itself an rclpy.Node and injects itself into every ROS-aware node of the tree at set_tree() time. The nodes then need no ros_node= at construction either.

docs.title: Adding custom nodes
docs.text:
bteng-nav2 nodes are regular bteng nodes. Mix them with any custom ActionNode, ConditionNode, or StatefulActionNode:

from bteng import ActionNode, NodeStatus

class LogGoalNode(ActionNode):
    @classmethod
    def provided_ports(cls):
        from bteng import InputPort
        return [InputPort("goal_pose")]

    def tick(self):
        goal = self.get_input("goal_pose")
        print(f"Goal: x={goal.pose.position.x}, y={goal.pose.position.y}")
        return NodeStatus.SUCCESS

log_config = NodeConfig(
    blackboard=bb,
    input_ports={"goal_pose": "goal_pose"},
)
log_node = LogGoalNode("log_goal", config=log_config)

sequence = SequenceNode("main", children=[log_node, navigate])

Custom nodes that do not call ROS 2 do not need ros_node.

docs.title: Running trees from the command line
docs.text:
A project that uses bteng-nav2 needs no application Python. The trees are XML, the poses and tuning values are YAML, and bteng-nav2 run supplies the ROS lifecycle, the tick loop, the failure report and the exit code.

bteng-nav2 run trees/ -p params.yaml                  # every *.xml in a directory
bteng-nav2 run trees/patrol.xml -p params.yaml        # one tree
bteng-nav2 run trees/ -p params.yaml --dry-run        # build only, no robot
bteng-nav2 nodes                                      # list the XML tags

A project layout ends up looking like this — the same shape as a bteng-opcua project:

Path Written by Purpose params.yaml hand namespace, use_sim_time, poses, tuning values trees/*.xml hand the behavior trees — — there is no application Python

docs.title: The params file
docs.text:
ros:
  namespace: /robot1          # optional, default ""
  node_name: bteng_nav2       # optional, the rclpy node the tree nodes share
  use_sim_time: true          # optional, default false

blackboard:
  goal_pose:    {type: pose, frame_id: map, x: 2.0, y: 1.5, yaw: 0.0}
  initial_pose: {type: pose_cov, frame_id: map, x: 0.0, y: 0.0, yaw: 0.0}
  waypoints:    {type: poses, frame_id: map, points: [[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0, 1.57]]}
  backup_dist:  0.30          # scalars pass straight through
  dock_id:      "dock_a"

Everything under blackboard: is seeded before each tree runs. That is the whole point of the file: a BT XML attribute is a string, but NavigateToPoseNode.goal_pose wants a geometry_msgs/PoseStamped. The params file builds the message; the tree only references the key.

docs.title: Value types
docs.text:
type: Message Keys pose geometry_msgs/PoseStamped frame_id="map", x, y, z, yaw or qx/qy/qz/qw pose_cov geometry_msgs/PoseWithCovarianceStamped pose keys + covariance (36 numbers) poses list[PoseStamped] frame_id, points: — [x, y], [x, y, yaw], or a pose mapping path nav_msgs/Path frame_id, points: (same forms) point geometry_msgs/Point x, y, z quaternion geometry_msgs/Quaternion yaw or qx/qy/qz/qw duration builtin_interfaces/Duration sec/nanosec, or float seconds

Yaw-only orientation: z = sin(yaw/2), w = cos(yaw/2). header.stamp is left at zero — there is no ROS clock when the file is read, and Nav2 reads a zero stamp as "now".

Validation is strict on purpose. A mapping without a type:, an unknown type:, an unknown key inside a spec, or a covariance that is not 36 numbers is an error naming the offending blackboard key. A typo'd fram_id must not silently fall back to map.

Anything that is not a mapping — numbers, strings, bools, lists of scalars — passes through unchanged.

docs.title: The tree files
docs.text:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<BTEng format_version="1.0" main_tree_to_execute="main">
  <Tree ID="main">
    <Fallback name="navigate_with_recovery">

      <NavigateToPose name="attempt" goal_pose="{goal_pose}" result="{nav_result}" />

      <Sequence name="recover_and_retry">
        <ClearGlobalCostmap name="clear" />
        <BackUp name="back_off" backup_dist="{backup_dist}" />
        <NavigateToPose name="retry" goal_pose="{goal_pose}" />
      </Sequence>

    </Fallback>
  </Tree>
</BTEng>

attr="{key}" is a blackboard reference; attr="value" is a static value. Control nodes (Sequence, Fallback, Parallel, ReactiveSequence, …) and decorators (Inverter, Retry, Timeout, RateController, ForceSuccess, ForceFailure) come from BTEng itself. SetBlackboard and CheckBlackboard are registered for you — BTEng ships them but does not auto-register them as XML tags.

docs.title: Tag names
docs.text: Every node has two tags: the short form and the Python class name. NavigateToPose and NavigateToPoseNode are the same node; IsBatteryLow and IsBatteryLowCondition likewise. The short form makes hand-written XML read like upstream Nav2 BT XML. bteng-nav2 nodes lists all of them, and --long adds each node's ROS action/service/topic name.

docs.title: Output ports need no declaration
docs.text: In plain BTEng XML, path="{path}" on a node that writes path would bind as an input unless the file carries a <TreeNodesModel> block. bteng-nav2 seeds the parser's port directions from each node's own provided_ports(), so a {key} attribute binds the way the node declared it. A <TreeNodesModel> block in the file still wins if you write one.

docs.title: --dry-run — the CI gate
docs.text:
bteng-nav2 run trees/ -p params.yaml --dry-run --plain

Parses every tree, resolves every tag, validates every seeded value, prints the tree structure and what each blackboard key would become, and exits non-zero if anything failed. No ROS context is created, nothing is contacted, nothing ticks — so a broken tree or a mistyped pose fails in a pipeline instead of on a robot.

It needs no ROS installation at all: not a running graph, not rclpy, not the message packages. The params are validated rather than built — an unknown key, a yaw/quaternion conflict, an unnormalized quaternion or a wrong-length covariance is still caught — so a typed key reports as pose (validated, not built) rather than as a constructed PoseStamped. Drop --dry-run and the same file builds real messages, which does require the message packages.

docs.title: Multi-robot: --namespace
docs.text:
bteng-nav2 run trees/ -p params.yaml --namespace /robot1

Every bteng-nav2 node declares an absolute ROS name (/navigate_to_pose), and absolute names ignore a node's namespace — so the names are rewritten explicitly at tree-build time: /navigate_to_pose → /robot1/navigate_to_pose. Both the node attribute and the matching params entry are rewritten, because a few nodes recompute their service name in on_start(). Relative and already-namespaced names are left alone, so the rewrite is idempotent.

Endpoints bound to a blackboard key (action_name="{planner_action}") are rewritten too — the value in the blackboard, not just the attribute — so a params file that names a server does not quietly escape the namespace.

One exception: SetCostmapParameterNode and GetCostmapParameterNode derive /{ros_node_name}/set_parameters from a port, and namespacing that would be guesswork. Write the namespaced value into the port instead.

To point one node somewhere else without moving the whole tree, set its endpoint port directly: action_name, service_name or topic_name. See Retargeting endpoints.

docs.title: Flags
docs.text:
Flag Default Meaning -p, --params ./params.yaml if it exists Params YAML. An explicitly named file that does not exist is an error --bb KEY=VALUE — Seed or override one blackboard key; repeatable. YAML-typed, so --bb enabled=false is a bool and --bb n=5 is an int. A mapping is built like a params entry: --bb 'goal_pose={type: pose, x: 3.0}' --namespace from params Override ros.namespace --timeout 60 Per-tree timeout in seconds. On expiry the tree is halted and reported FAILURE --tick-interval 0.05 Tick period in seconds (20 Hz) --dry-run off Build only --plain off No colour, no emoji — for log files and CI --log INFO DEBUG / INFO / WARNING

Exit code is 0 only if every tree ended in SUCCESS. One broken tree becomes a FAILURE result and never aborts the batch, so a directory run always reports on all of its trees.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
── 04_recovery.xml ──
🌳 04_recovery.xml started (timeout=60.0s)
🧭 ✅ attempt
🎉 04_recovery.xml finished: SUCCESS

=== Summary ===
  ✅ 04_recovery.xml         SUCCESS

One line per leaf as it settles, then a summary. Colour and emoji live only in the run command — the node classes log plain logging records under bteng_nav2.*, so file and CI logs stay clean. --plain turns the decoration off entirely.

docs.title: Calling it from Python instead
docs.text:
The CLI is a thin wrapper; the same three pieces are importable:

from bteng_nav2.config import load_config
from bteng_nav2.runtime import install_logging, run_trees
from bteng_nav2.xml_integration import load_tree, register_nodes

install_logging("INFO")                       # only the app layer configures logging
exit_code = run_trees(["trees/"], "params.yaml", presets=["backup_dist=0.5"], timeout=120.0)

register_nodes() + load_tree(path, blackboard=bb) is the low-level pair if you want to build the tree yourself and drive it with your own executor — see Building Trees.

docs.title: Condition nodes
docs.text: Condition nodes evaluate a runtime state and return SUCCESS or FAILURE on every tick. In a SequenceNode a failing condition short-circuits execution before the action nodes run. In a FallbackNode a succeeding condition short-circuits the remaining branches.

docs.title: IsRobotNearGoalCondition
docs.text:
Source: bteng_nav2.conditions.pose Topic: /amcl_pose (geometry_msgs/PoseWithCovarianceStamped)

Returns SUCCESS when the Euclidean distance between the robot's current AMCL pose and goal_pose is less than tolerance metres. Returns FAILURE otherwise.

Ports

Name Direction Default Description goal_pose IN — PoseStamped target to measure distance to tolerance IN "0.5" Acceptable distance in metres (string-cast float)

Example

from bteng_nav2 import IsRobotNearGoalCondition

bb.set("goal_pose", make_goal("map", x=2.0, y=1.5))
bb.set("tolerance", 0.3)

config = NodeConfig(
    blackboard=bb,
    input_ports={
        "goal_pose": "goal_pose",
        "tolerance": "tolerance",
    },
)
near_goal = IsRobotNearGoalCondition("near_goal", config=config, ros_node=ros_node)

Place this inside a FallbackNode before the navigation node. When the robot is already within tolerance of the goal the condition returns SUCCESS and the fallback skips navigation entirely.

docs.title: IsLocalizationActiveCondition
docs.text:
Source: bteng_nav2.conditions.pose Topic: /amcl_pose (geometry_msgs/PoseWithCovarianceStamped)

Returns SUCCESS when an AMCL pose message has been received within the last timeout seconds. Returns FAILURE if no message has arrived within that window, indicating that localization may have died or not yet started.

Ports

Name Direction Default Description timeout IN "2.0" Maximum age in seconds of the last received AMCL pose

Example

from bteng_nav2 import IsLocalizationActiveCondition

bb.set("amcl_timeout", 2.0)

config = NodeConfig(
    blackboard=bb,
    input_ports={"timeout": "amcl_timeout"},
)
loc_check = IsLocalizationActiveCondition("loc_check", config=config, ros_node=ros_node)

Use this as the first child of a navigation sequence to fail fast before sending a goal when AMCL is not running.

docs.title: IsObstacleNearCondition
docs.text:
Source: bteng_nav2.conditions.obstacle Topic: /scan (sensor_msgs/LaserScan)

Returns SUCCESS when the closest valid laser scan reading is less than min_distance metres away. Returns FAILURE when all readings are farther than the threshold or the scan contains no valid ranges.

Ports

Name Direction Default Description min_distance IN "0.5" Obstacle detection threshold in metres

Example

from bteng_nav2 import IsObstacleNearCondition

bb.set("obstacle_threshold", 0.4)

config = NodeConfig(
    blackboard=bb,
    input_ports={"min_distance": "obstacle_threshold"},
)
obstacle_check = IsObstacleNearCondition("obstacle", config=config, ros_node=ros_node)

Place this condition in a reactive fallback around a navigation action to trigger recovery as soon as an obstacle enters the scan range.

docs.title: IsStuckCondition
docs.text:
Source: bteng_nav2.conditions.obstacle Topic: /odom (nav_msgs/Odometry)

Returns SUCCESS when both linear (vx) and angular (wz) velocity have been near zero for longer than stuck_timeout seconds, indicating the robot is not moving. Returns FAILURE while the robot is moving or the timeout has not elapsed.

Ports

Name Direction Default Description stuck_timeout IN "3.0" Time in seconds with near-zero velocity before declaring stuck

Example

from bteng_nav2 import IsStuckCondition

bb.set("stuck_timeout", 5.0)

config = NodeConfig(
    blackboard=bb,
    input_ports={"stuck_timeout": "stuck_timeout"},
)
stuck_check = IsStuckCondition("stuck", config=config, ros_node=ros_node)

Use this condition to detect a stalled navigation action and trigger a recovery branch.

docs.title: IsGoalUpdatedCondition
docs.text:
Source: bteng_nav2.conditions.nav_status Topic: none (pure blackboard comparison)

Returns SUCCESS when the goal_pose blackboard value has changed since the last call, by comparing a hash of the serialised value. Returns FAILURE when the goal is unchanged. Does not require a ROS node.

Ports

Name Direction Default Description goal_pose IN — PoseStamped to watch for changes

Example

from bteng_nav2 import IsGoalUpdatedCondition

config = NodeConfig(
    blackboard=bb,
    input_ports={"goal_pose": "goal_pose"},
)
goal_updated = IsGoalUpdatedCondition("goal_updated", config=config)

Use this at the top of a tree that receives goals dynamically. When the goal changes the condition returns SUCCESS, triggering a new navigation action. When the goal is the same the condition returns FAILURE, short-circuiting repeat goals.

docs.title: IsNavigationActiveCondition
docs.text:
Source: bteng_nav2.conditions.nav_status Topic: none (action server readiness check)

Returns SUCCESS when the /navigate_to_pose action server is ready to accept goals. Returns FAILURE when the server is not yet available.

Ports

This node has no ports.

Example

from bteng_nav2 import IsNavigationActiveCondition, NavigateToPoseNode
from bteng import SequenceNode

nav_active_config = NodeConfig(blackboard=bb)
nav_active = IsNavigationActiveCondition("nav_active", config=nav_active_config, ros_node=ros_node)

navigate_config = NodeConfig(
    blackboard=bb,
    input_ports={"goal_pose": "goal_pose"},
    output_ports={"result": "nav_result"},
)
navigate = NavigateToPoseNode("navigate", config=navigate_config, ros_node=ros_node)

# Sequence: check server, then send goal
nav_sequence = SequenceNode("nav_sequence", children=[nav_active, navigate])

docs.title: Retargeting endpoints
docs.text:
Every node in this package ships with a default ROS endpoint — NavigateToPoseNode talks to /navigate_to_pose, ClearGlobalCostmapNode to /global_costmap/clear_entirely_global_costmap. Those defaults are what make a tree readable: a tag and a goal, no plumbing.

They are also the two things most likely to be wrong on your stack: a second planner, a second controller, a per-robot namespace, or a distribution that renamed a service. This page is how you change them without writing Python.

docs.title: The endpoint port
docs.text:
Action, service and condition nodes each declare an input port carrying their endpoint:

Node kind Port Default comes from Action (RosActionNode) action_name the class attribute Service (RosServiceNode) service_name the class attribute Condition (RosConditionNode) topic_name the class attribute

Say nothing and the node behaves exactly as before. Set the attribute in XML and that node — only that node — is retargeted:

<Sequence name="two_planners">
  <ComputePathToPose name="plan_a" goal="{goal}" path="{path_a}"
                     action_name="/planner_a/compute_path_to_pose" />
  <ComputePathToPose name="plan_b" goal="{goal}" path="{path_b}"
                     action_name="/planner_b/compute_path_to_pose" />
</Sequence>

<IsObstacleNear name="rear" topic_name="/scan_rear" min_distance="0.4" />

It is an ordinary port, so it can also come from the blackboard, which means from the params file:

blackboard:
  planner_action: /planner_b/compute_path_to_pose

<ComputePathToPose name="plan" goal="{goal}" path="{path}"
                   action_name="{planner_action}" />

The port is declared by bteng-ros2 on the base classes, so all 38 node types have it without any of them mentioning it. A node that declares the port itself keeps its own declaration.

docs.title: Namespaces
docs.text:
Node endpoints are absolute names (/navigate_to_pose, leading slash), and an absolute name ignores the ROS node's namespace. Setting a namespace on the process therefore does nothing at all to them. --namespace rewrites the names at build time instead:

bteng-nav2 run trees/ -p params.yaml --namespace /robot1

/navigate_to_pose becomes /robot1/navigate_to_pose, and so does every other absolute endpoint in the tree, including publisher topics and the endpoint values bound through the blackboard. One set of trees drives any number of robots.

Two exceptions, both worth knowing before you rely on the rewrite:

  • SetCostmapParameterNode / GetCostmapParameterNode build /{ros_node_name}/set_parameters from a port, so there is no absolute attribute to rewrite. Write the namespaced node name into the port yourself.
  • Publisher nodes (PublishGoalPoseNode, SetInitialPoseNode) are rewritten by --namespace but have no per-node endpoint port — RosTopicMixin is not hooked the way the three base classes above are. Retargeting one inside a namespace needs a subclass.

docs.title: Check the names against your distribution
docs.text:
Nav2 has renamed endpoints between distributions, and a wrong name is invisible until you have a robot: the client is created, the goal is built, every offline test passes, and the first tick waits for a server that will never appear.

Seven of this package's defaults were wrong until 0.2.3 — they named servers that exist nowhere in Nav2:

Node Was Is ClearGlobalCostmapNode /clear_costmap_global_srv /global_costmap/clear_entirely_global_costmap ClearLocalCostmapNode /clear_costmap_local_srv /local_costmap/clear_entirely_local_costmap ClearGlobalCostmapAroundRobotNode /clear_global_costmap_around_robot /global_costmap/clear_around_global_costmap ClearLocalCostmapAroundRobotNode /clear_local_costmap_around_robot /local_costmap/clear_around_local_costmap GetGlobalCostmapNode /get_costmap_global /global_costmap/get_costmap GetLocalCostmapNode /get_costmap_local /local_costmap/get_costmap BackUpNode /back_up /backup

The costmap services are namespaced by their costmap because each costmap node creates its own set. BackUpNode's server is declared backup in nav2_behaviors; the action type is BackUp, which is where the wrong name came from.

Verify against the stack you actually have, not against this table:

ros2 action list | grep -E 'navigate|compute|follow|spin|backup'
ros2 service list | grep costmap

Then fix any mismatch in the tree with the endpoint port — no code change, no release.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
A client created microseconds ago is not a client that can reach anything: DDS discovery has not finished. bteng-ros2 waits for the server to appear, spread across ticks rather than blocking, up to discovery_timeout (5.0 s by default). Without that wait every service node fails its first tick against a real graph while passing every stubbed test.

If a node times out waiting, the endpoint is the first thing to check — a name nothing serves and a stack that is not running look identical from inside the node.

docs.title: Publisher nodes
docs.text:
Publisher nodes publish a single ROS 2 message to a topic and return SUCCESS immediately. They are useful for initialising system state before a navigation tree runs — for example, sending an initial pose to AMCL or forwarding a goal pose to a visualisation tool.

Both nodes inherit from RosTopicMixin and ActionNode. A ros_node is not required at construction: RosBTExecutor injects itself into every ROS-aware node when it starts.

Both wait for a subscriber to match before publishing, up to match_timeout (2.0 s), and publish once per activation. A publisher created and published to in the same tick puts its message nowhere — DDS has not matched the subscriber yet — while the node still reports SUCCESS. That is exactly how an /initialpose publication is lost and AMCL never localises.

These two are the exception to Retargeting endpoints: action, service and condition nodes inherit an endpoint port from their base class, but RosTopicMixin has no such hook, so a publisher's topic is a class attribute only. --namespace still rewrites it; pointing one at a different topic in the same namespace needs a subclass.

docs.title: PublishGoalPoseNode
docs.text:
Publish a PoseStamped message to /goal_pose and return SUCCESS.

Source: bteng_nav2.publishers.goal Topic: /goal_pose (geometry_msgs/PoseStamped)

Ports

docs.title: Service nodes
docs.text:
Service nodes wrap Nav2 ROS 2 service clients. Each node sends a request, returns RUNNING while waiting for the response, and returns SUCCESS or FAILURE based on the service response.

All service nodes inherit from RosServiceNode. A ros_node is not required at construction: RosBTExecutor injects itself into every ROS-aware node when it starts. Pass ros_node= yourself only to override that.

Before its first request each node waits for the service server to appear, because DDS discovery has not finished at the moment a client is created — without that wait every service node fails its first tick against a real graph. Each node's server is settable per node through a service_name port; see Retargeting endpoints.

docs.title: IsPathValidNode
docs.text:
Check whether a given path is collision-free by calling the /is_path_valid service. Returns SUCCESS if the path is valid and FAILURE if the path contains a collision or the service call fails.

Ports

Name Direction Default Description path IN — nav_msgs/Path to validate

Example

Combine with ComputePathToPoseNode in a sequence to validate before following:

from bteng import SequenceNode
from bteng_nav2 import ComputePathToPoseNode, IsPathValidNode, FollowPathNode

compute_config = NodeConfig(
    blackboard=bb,
    input_ports={"goal": "goal"},
    output_ports={"path": "path"},
)
compute = ComputePathToPoseNode("compute", config=compute_config, ros_node=ros_node)

validate_config = NodeConfig(
    blackboard=bb,
    input_ports={"path": "path"},
)
validate = IsPathValidNode("validate", config=validate_config, ros_node=ros_node)

follow_config = NodeConfig(
    blackboard=bb,
    input_ports={"path": "path"},
)
follow = FollowPathNode("follow", config=follow_config, ros_node=ros_node)

pipeline = SequenceNode("pipeline", children=[compute, validate, follow])

docs.title: Testing without ROS 2
docs.text: bteng-nav2 ships a conftest.py that stubs the entire ROS 2 Python API so the test suite runs on any machine without a ROS installation. This page explains how the stubs work and how to write your own tests.

docs.title: How conftest.py stubs work
docs.text:
The file at test/conftest.py is loaded automatically by pytest before any test module. It calls a series of _mock_*() functions that insert fake module objects directly into sys.modules. When a bteng-nav2 node later executes import rclpy or from nav2_msgs.action import NavigateToPose, Python finds the stub module in sys.modules rather than attempting to import the real package.

The stub modules provide:

  • rclpy — init, shutdown, Node, ActionClient, Future, QoSProfile, and executor classes
  • nav2_msgs.action — goal, result, and feedback stub classes for all Nav2 actions
  • nav2_msgs.srv — request and response stubs for all Nav2 services
  • geometry_msgs.msg — PoseStamped, PoseWithCovarianceStamped, Twist, and related types
  • nav_msgs.msg — Path, Odometry, OccupancyGrid
  • sensor_msgs.msg — LaserScan, PointCloud2
  • opennav_docking_msgs.action — DockRobot, UndockRobot

All stub classes have the same attribute structure as the real messages but contain no ROS runtime behaviour.

docs.title: Running pytest offline
docs.text:
With the stubs in place, run the full test suite without sourcing ROS 2:

# From the repository root
pytest tests/ -v

Run a single file:

pytest tests/test_actions.py -v
pytest tests/test_conditions.py -v

Tests that exercise action or service nodes construct nodes directly and call on_start() and make_goal() or make_request() without spinning an executor, because the stub ActionClient and ServiceClient return dummy futures.

docs.title: Writing a node test
docs.text:
The recommended pattern is to construct the node, call lifecycle methods directly, and assert on blackboard state.

import pytest
from bteng import Blackboard, NodeConfig

# conftest.py is already loaded by pytest; no import needed

def test_navigate_to_pose_make_goal():
    from bteng_nav2 import NavigateToPoseNode

    bb = Blackboard()

    # Build a stub PoseStamped using the stubbed geometry_msgs
    from geometry_msgs.msg import PoseStamped
    pose = PoseStamped()
    pose.header.frame_id = "map"
    pose.pose.position.x = 1.0
    pose.pose.position.y = 2.0

    bb.set("goal_pose", pose)

    config = NodeConfig(
        blackboard=bb,
        input_ports={"goal_pose": "goal_pose"},
        output_ports={"result": "nav_result"},
    )

    # ros_node is not called during make_goal(); pass None for unit tests
    node = NavigateToPoseNode("navigate", config=config, ros_node=None)

    goal = node.make_goal()
    assert goal.pose.pose.position.x == 1.0
    assert goal.pose.pose.position.y == 2.0

docs.title: Integration tests with FakeRosNode
docs.text:
For higher-level tests that exercise the full tick loop, bteng-ros2 provides FakeRosNode. It behaves like a real rclpy.node.Node but does not connect to a DDS network.

from bteng_ros2.testing import FakeRosNode
from bteng import Blackboard, NodeConfig, Tree
from bteng_ros2 import RosBTExecutor
from bteng_nav2 import IsGoalUpdatedCondition

def test_goal_updated_condition():
    ros_node = FakeRosNode("test_node")
    bb = Blackboard()

    from geometry_msgs.msg import PoseStamped
    pose_a = PoseStamped()
    pose_a.pose.position.x = 1.0
    bb.set("goal_pose", pose_a)

    config = NodeConfig(
        blackboard=bb,
        input_ports={"goal_pose": "goal_pose"},
    )
    condition = IsGoalUpdatedCondition("goal_check", config=config)

    from bteng import NodeStatus
    # First tick: goal changed (from nothing to pose_a)
    assert condition.tick() == NodeStatus.SUCCESS

    # Second tick: goal unchanged
    assert condition.tick() == NodeStatus.FAILURE

    # Update the goal
    pose_b = PoseStamped()
    pose_b.pose.position.x = 2.0
    bb.set("goal_pose", pose_b)

    # Third tick: goal changed again
    assert condition.tick() == NodeStatus.SUCCESS

IsGoalUpdatedCondition is a pure blackboard condition and does not need ros_node, making it the simplest node to test in isolation.
